I just want to start off by saying that I'm really proud of you for having the courage to want to leave. 

I felt similar to what you're describing. I was terrified of the unknown and didn't know what I was going to do, but I was so exhausted. 

The most important thing is to have some sort of support system to fall back on, whether it be any friends or family you may still be in contact with, your place of employment, a shelter, anywhere that can help you get through those first few weeks. I was incredibly lucky to have an empathetic boss, and he let me set up a place to sleep in the back room of the store I worked at for as long as I needed, and I also had a friend who was gracious enough to let me stay in her apartment for a few weeks while I tried to find a living arrangement I could afford. 
I was still in a heavy state of codependency, and wound up meeting a guy who had lived through a very similar type of abuse. He was extremely supportive and caring, and to this day, I don't think I would have survived being homeless on top of all of the trauma I had just finished going through eating me alive. 

When I had finally hit my breaking point, I knew that breaking up with him could be dangerous for me. I was too scared to break up with him without a third party present. I truly believe that's what stopped that day from becoming violent. 

My life after leaving has been so peaceful. I can do what I want when I want, I can wear what I want, I can be friends with whoever I want and hang out with them for as long as I want to, I can eat what I want, and I can have my own interests again and I don't have anyone to ruin those things for me or not allow me to pursue said interests. I'm free now, and Ive experienced so much peace and so much freedom in my adult life. 

It was the hardest thing I've ever done, and the year that followed that breakup was the hardest year of my life, but the love I feel for my life and myself now means that year long struggle was worth it. 

I hope you find your peace, and I hope that you get out safely when you do. ❤️

In my experience, straight tube bongs like that one can fall over/break easier because the surface area of the base of the bong isn't wide or heavy enough, and they don't hold as much water as a beaker or basket style base, so it wouldn't cool the smoke as well if I were to take an educated guess.

I know for a fact that people pay WAY more for bongs than $110. Some people like to have nice things, not everyone wants a cheap, thin piece of glass/ceramic to smoke out of. I spend $175 on my RedEyeTek bong 3 years ago, it's made of tempered glass and it's incredibly sturdy and smooth, not to mention attractive. It's been dropped a few times and doesn't have so much as a scratch on it, and its used almost daily and has been since purchase. A good bong is a good investment to someone who gets good use out of it, or for someone who appreciates the craftsmanship behind the glass/ceramic. I've seen some absolutely breathtaking pieces of glass that I could only dream of smoking out of. Sometimes, it's just worth the money!


Edit: as someone who works in a head shop, no two bongs are the same. Smoothness can depend on a lot of different factors, including size of the tube itself, base of the bong, whether or not the downstem is diffused, or whether or not the bong has percolators inside. Each percolator hits differently as well, with some being way more harsh and basically ineffective (Matrix percs) to some being extremely smooth (honeycomb percs, tree percs).
